content: The following references provide detailed insights into various aspects of breastfeeding practices, interventions, and healthcare support systems: 1. Ujo Mde F and Soares Schmitz Bde A conducted a reassessment of Baby-Friendly Hospitals in Brazil, published in the Journal of Human Lactation in 2007, highlighting the implementation and outcomes of breastfeeding-friendly policies in healthcare facilities. 2. Moore T, Gauld R, and Williams S examined the implementation of the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative (BFHI) in New Zealand public hospitals, as reported in the International Breastfeeding Journal in 2007, focusing on policy adherence and its impact on breastfeeding rates. 3. Duffy EP, Percival P, and Kershaw E demonstrated the positive effects of antenatal group teaching sessions on reducing postnatal nipple pain, trauma, and improving breastfeeding rates, as published in Midwifery in 1997. 4. Kronborg H, Maimburg RD, and Væth M conducted a randomized trial on antenatal training to enhance breastfeeding outcomes, published in Midwifery in 2012, emphasizing the importance of prenatal education. 5. Yotebieng M et al. evaluated the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding program in the Democratic Republic of Congo, showing its effectiveness in promoting early initiation and exclusive breastfeeding, as reported in The Lancet Global Health in 2015. 6. McLachlan HL et al. assessed the Supporting Breastfeeding in Local Communities (SILC) initiative in Victoria, Australia, through a cluster-randomized controlled trial, published in BMJ Open in 2016, highlighting community-based breastfeeding support. 7. Pérez-Escamilla R and Hall Moran V discussed the challenges of scaling up breastfeeding programs in complex adaptive systems, as detailed in Maternal and Child Nutrition in 2016. 8. Semenic S et al. conducted an integrative review on barriers, facilitators, and recommendations for implementing the Baby-Friendly Initiative (BFI), published in the Journal of Human Lactation in 2012. 9. Nyqvist KH et al. introduced the Neo-BFHI, an adaptation of the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative for neonatal wards, emphasizing three guiding principles to support breastfeeding, as outlined in a core document accessed in 2017. 10. Nyqvist KH et al. expanded the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding into neonatal intensive care settings, providing expert group recommendations, as published in the Journal of Human Lactation in 2012. 11. Pérez-Escamilla R and Sellen D explored equity in breastfeeding practices and proposed future directions, as discussed in the Journal of Human Lactation in 2015. 12. Zamora G et al. applied an equity lens to breastfeeding interventions, focusing on optimal breastfeeding practices, as reported in the Journal of Human Lactation in 2015. 13. The World Health Organization (WHO) provided guidelines for protecting, promoting, and supporting breastfeeding in maternity and newborn care facilities, accessible through their official website in 2017. 14. Guyatt G et al. introduced the GRADE guidelines for rating the quality of evidence and strength of recommendations, as published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology in 2011. 15. The GRADE Working Group developed systematic frameworks for evidence-based decision-making in clinical practice and public health, as detailed in BMJ in 2016. 16. Rea MF et al. assessed breastfeeding counseling knowledge and skills among healthcare providers in Brazil, as published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization in 1999. 17. Ekström A et al. demonstrated how process-oriented breastfeeding training altered healthcare professionals' attitudes, as reported in the Scandinavian Journal of Public Health. 18. Westphal MF et al. evaluated the impact of breastfeeding training for health professionals on institutional practices, as published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization in 1995. 19. Weddig J et al. explored hospital nurses' perspectives on best practices for breastfeeding initiation, as reported in the Journal of Obstetric, Gynecologic, and Neonatal Nursing in 2011. 20. Downie J et al. conducted a longitudinal study on enhancing nurses' and midwives' ability to promote breastfeeding, as published in Birth Issues in 2002. 21. Martens PJ examined the effects of breastfeeding education on nursing staff beliefs, exclusive breastfeeding rates, and Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative compliance in a rural Canadian hospital, as reported in the Journal of Human Lactation in 2000. 22. Lewin S et al. proposed using qualitative evidence in decision-making for health and social interventions, as outlined in PLoS Medicine in 2015. 23. Abolyan LV evaluated breastfeeding support in Baby-Friendly and non-Baby-Friendly hospitals in Russia, as published in Breastfeeding Medicine in 2006. 24. Aguilar Cordero MJ et al. studied breastfeeding practices in premature infants in Palestine, focusing on development-centered care, as reported in Nutr Hosp in 2012. 25. Carfoot S et al. conducted a randomized controlled trial on the effects of skin-to-skin care on breastfeeding in Northern England, as published in Midwifery in 2005. These studies collectively provide a comprehensive understanding of breastfeeding promotion, challenges, and interventions across diverse healthcare settings and populations.
